A multi-site qualitative study using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research","authors":"Nakamura-Obi E, Lindqvist-Mensah R, Carvalho-Doyle P","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Emergency Care Implementation","doi":"10.5555/jeci.2021.0152","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 58 staff in six emergency departments, three with consistently high and three with low rates of antibiotics within one hour for suspected sepsis, and coded the interviews with the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. High-performing departments had nurse-initiated antibiotic protocols, a sepsis champion on every shift and antibiotics stocked near triage. Low-performing departments relied on physician orders, described crowding and handover delays, and kept antibiotics in a pharmacy room away from triage. Staff at all sites knew the bundle well. Night shifts were described as the weakest point in low performers, where one physician covered the whole department."},{"title":"Variation in time to antibiotics for sepsis across a regional hospital network: a benchmarking report","authors":"Regional Sepsis Improvement Network","year":2019,"venue":"Regional Sepsis Improvement Network reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"This report compares time to antibiotics for adults with suspected sepsis across nine hospitals in one regional network over twelve months. The proportion of patients receiving antibiotics within one hour of recognition ranged from 41 to 86 percent between hospitals. In every hospital the proportion was lower at night and at weekends, and the gap between day and night was largest in the smaller hospitals. Hospitals differed in how recognition time was recorded, which limits comparison. The report does not examine reasons for the variation and recommends that hospitals with lower figures learn from those with higher figures."},{"title":"What helps and hinders timely sepsis bundle delivery in hospitals: a systematic review of 27 qualitative and mixed-methods studies","authors":"Adeyemi-Fairclough T, Borg-Haddad N, Sato-Keane L","year":2023,"venue":"Implementation in Acute Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/iacr.2023.0077","providerType":"review","abstract":"We synthesised 27 qualitative and mixed-methods studies of sepsis bundle delivery in hospitals. Across 27 studies, the most consistent barriers were crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering antibiotics and delayed access to antibiotics, and the most consistent facilitators were protocols allowing nurses to start treatment, visible leadership and regular feedback of performance. Confidence in these findings, assessed with GRADE-CERQual, was moderate for most themes and low for leadership. Few studies compared high- and low-performing sites directly, and night-time care was rarely examined separately. The authors recommend comparative designs that explain variation between sites."},{"title":"Nurse-initiated sepsis protocols and time to antibiotics: a stepped introduction across four emergency departments","authors":"Whitlock-Ogunleye S, Dahl-Vasquez M","year":2020,"venue":"Morrowvale Emergency Nursing Reports","doi":"10.5555/enpr.2020.0231","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Four emergency departments introduced a protocol allowing triage nurses to start antibiotics for suspected sepsis, one department every three months. Across the four departments, median time from triage to antibiotics fell from 94 to 58 minutes after the protocol started. The fall was greatest in departments where pharmacy stocked antibiotics in the emergency department, and smallest where nurses reported low confidence in using the protocol without a physician present. Night-time performance improved less than daytime performance. The introduction was not randomised and other changes happened at the same time, so the size of the effect is uncertain."}]}
